title: Quantum quenches of scar states in the Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki model via Clifford augmented tensor network simulation
authors: Azar C. Nakhl, Ben Harper, Muhammad Usman, Thomas Quella
abstract: Clifford augmented methods have emerged as a powerful technique to simulate quantum circuits and many-body systems by exploiting the stabiliser structure found in said systems, whilst additionally enabling one to readily quantify the non-stabilizerness (i.e.\ magic) present. In this work, we utilise a qudit Clifford augmented simulation method to probe the presence of magic in the Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) model, finding that its ground state and scar states are highly magical as quantified by their Stabiliser Rényi Entropy (SRE). Nevertheless, owing to its low entanglement structure, these states are still readily expressible as a Clifford augmented Matrix Product State with low bond-dimension and moreover may be time-evolved using the Clifford augmented time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) algorithm. We utilise Clifford augmented TDVP to study the string order dynamics in the scar states of the AKLT model after a quench within the Haldane phase to the anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian. We observe that there is a decay of string order following the quench, which is more pronounced with increasing bimagnon number. This finding highlights the sensitivity of string order in the AKLT scar states to symmetry-preserving quenches, even when the initial and final Hamiltonians belong to the same topological phase.
summary: This work uses advanced Clifford augmented tensor network simulations to study quantum quenches in the AKLT model. The authors find that while the initial scar states are highly non-stabilizible, the string order decays after the quench, revealing sensitivity to symmetry changes. This demonstrates the utility of the Clifford augmented TDVP for analyzing topological properties in complex quantum systems.
main_problem: To investigate the stability and dynamics of scar states in the AKLT model following a quantum quench, while quantifying the underlying non-stabilizerness ('magic').
main_result: The study observes a decay of string order after the quench, which is sensitive to symmetry-preserving changes, even when remaining within the same topological phase.
method: The research employs a Clifford augmented Time-Dependent Variational Principle (TDVP) algorithm implemented via tensor networks to simulate the time evolution of the quantum state.
model_or_system: The system is the spin-1 Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) model, which is studied through its ground and scar states. Dynamics are simulated by quenching the system to the anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian.
key_observables: String order parameter, Stabilizer Rényi Entropy (SRE) quantifying non-stabilizerness, and the decay rate of string order.
important_parameters: The quench process itself, the bimagnon number, and the bond dimension ($\chi$) used in the tensor network simulation.
main_assumptions: The simulation relies on the assumption that the Clifford augmented TDVP method accurately captures the dynamics, although long-time simulations require prohibitively large bond dimensions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Clifford augmented simulation procedure, including scar state preparation and the 2-site TDVP evolution steps.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the Clifford augmented simulation framework for probing non-stabilizerness (SRE) in the AKLT model. It then applies this method to study the string order dynamics following a quench from the AKLT Hamiltonian to the Heisenberg Hamiltonian.
why_interesting: The combination of advanced tensor network techniques (Clifford augmentation) with the study of topological order (string order) and non-stabilizerness provides a powerful, modern tool for analyzing quantum many-body dynamics.

(a) A plot of the approximate NsEE (in red) and SRE (in blue) and (b) a plot of the Entanglement entropy (in red) and SRE (in blue) for the AKLT ground state and tower of scar states for N = 50 sites. The bimagnon number n labels each of the scar states, with the ground state given by n = 0. We find that SRE peaks first at about n = 9 with entangle- ment entropy peaking at the already established n = N/4 [33]. The approximate NsEE continues to grow until n = 15, indi- cating sub-optimal disentangling with GCAMPS. Note that the approximate NsEE serves as a measure of computational complexity and is distinct from the true NsEE which like SRE grows with increasing non-stabilizerness.
